# Literature Review {#sec-literature}

## Relation to Fu (2006)

@fu2006 is the closest benchmark. Fu studies a two-player Tullock contest with one informed and one uninformed player. When the informed player leads, equilibrium may be separating, pooling, or semi-separating; when the uninformed player leads, the informed follower responds to the observed action. The mechanism is simple: informed effort is a signal, and the follower updates beliefs.

This paper makes two changes. Labor's winning value $V_L$ is private information, while management's value $V$ is common knowledge; and management's best response depends on effort and $V$, not on posterior beliefs. This shuts down Fu's signaling-belief-response channel and makes separation unique in LM. The type distribution is also generalized beyond the binary case. Timing is governed by four one-deviation gaps: $\Delta_L^{\mathrm{ML}}$, $\Delta_L^{\mathrm{LM}}$, $\Delta_M^{\mathrm{ML}}$, and $\Delta_M^{\mathrm{SS}}$.

## Relation to Endogenous-Timing Literature

Classic endogenous-timing results suggest that weak players lead and strong players wait; see @hamilton1990 and @fu2006. Later work qualifies this benchmark. @hoffmann2012 allows generalized success functions and endogenous prizes; @baikleelee2022 studies three-player Tullock contests; @dengfuwuzhu2021 finds second-mover advantages in sequential all-pay contests.

This paper gives a tractable two-player benchmark with one-sided private information and closed-form type-level timing conditions.

## Relation to Asymmetric-Information and Signaling Literature

The paper also connects to incomplete-information contests. @hurley1998, @warneryd2003, and @warneryd2012 study how value uncertainty changes effort. @fu2006 remains closest because effort itself is a signal. Here, effort signaling does not merely allow separation; it makes separation unique in LM.

Other papers add pre-contest communication. @fu2013 studies public messages as commitment and signals; @dentermorgansisak2022 studies costly signals of capability. This paper adds no communication technology: equilibrium effort is the only signal.

## Relation to Recent Extensions

Recent studies show that added frictions can reverse timing predictions. @protopappas2023 studies manipulation of move-order rules. @protopappas2025 shows that cost uncertainty may make strong players lead. @dentersisak2015 shows that uncertainty about resolve weakens deterrence.

The lesson is that timing depends on which state variable is private: valuation, future cost, resolve, or institutional options. This paper isolates private valuation and derives sharp type-level ordering.

## Bottom Line

The paper is best read as an analytical extension of @fu2006: not more players or richer timing, but sharper conditions for first- versus second-mover incentives.
